The circular field around a current is the familiar picture; the tensor is the covariant one.

title: Definition
body: The electromagnetic field is the unified relativistic field whose frame-dependent components are the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} and \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field}. Covariantly, it is represented by the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}.

title: Derivation
body:
The unified electromagnetic field is obtained conceptually by collecting the electric and magnetic components into the antisymmetric tensor \(F_{\mu
u}\). In a chosen frame, \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} components occupy the time-space part of the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}, while \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field} components occupy the spatial antisymmetric part. Under \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations}, those components mix, so the covariant object is the tensor, not the separate three-vectors. \optional_details{Why \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) mix under boosts}{A Lorentz boost mixes time and space coordinates. Since the electric field comes from time-space components of \(F_{\mu
u}\) and the magnetic field from space-space components, a boost mixes those components too. Thus an observer moving relative to a charge-current distribution may split the same tensor into different electric and magnetic parts.} \optional_details{Why \(F_{\mu
u}\) is the covariant object}{The separate three-vectors \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) depend on how an observer slices spacetime into time plus space. The tensor \(F_{\mu
u}\) contains all six components in a single object with a definite Lorentz transformation law. That is why covariant equations are written using \(F_{\mu
u}\), then decomposed into \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) only after a frame is chosen.}

title: Explanation
body: The electromagnetic field is the unified physical field whose frame-dependent faces are \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\). This is more than a vocabulary upgrade. It explains why electric and magnetic effects transform into each other between observers, why the field can carry energy and momentum, and why a local field description replaces instantaneous action at a distance. A useful mental model is that \(F_{\mu\nu}\) is the underlying object, while \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) are what a particular observer reads off from it.

title: Definition
body: Maxwell's equations are the relativistic field equations governing the \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}. In covariant form they relate the antisymmetric \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} to the source \cref{Four-current}{sr.four_current}, while the homogeneous equations express the fact that the field tensor is built from a potential.

title: Derivation
body:
Maxwell's equations follow by applying the \cref{Euler-Lagrange equations}{sr.euler_lagrange_equations} to the electromagnetic \cref{Field Lagrangian}{sr.field_lagrangian}. With \(F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu\), a standard electromagnetic Lagrangian density is \[ \mathcal L=- rac{1}{4\mu_0}F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}-j_\mu A^\mu, \] using the \(+---\) metric convention. Varying the action with respect to the potential \(A_\mu\) gives the sourced Maxwell equation \[ \partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0 j^
u. \] The second half of Maxwell's equations follows from the definition of \(F_{\mu
u}\) itself: \[ \partial_\lambda F_{\mu
u}+\partial_\mu F_{
u\lambda}+\partial_
u F_{\lambda\mu}=0. \] Together these equations are local \cref{Field equations}{sr.field_equations}: at each spacetime event they relate field derivatives to the charge and current source at that event. \optional_details{Varying the electromagnetic Lagrangian}{The variation of \(F_{\mu
u}\) is \(\delta F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu\delta A_
u-\partial_
u\delta A_\mu\). Substituting this into the variation of \(-F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}/(4\mu_0)-j_\mu A^\mu\), integrating by parts, and discarding the boundary term leaves a coefficient multiplying \(\delta A_
u\). Setting that coefficient to zero gives \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0j^
u\), up to the chosen sign convention.} \optional_details{How \(F=dA\) gives the homogeneous equations}{Because \(F_{\mu
u}\) is built from derivatives of \(A_\mu\), the cyclic combination \(\partial_\lambda F_{\mu
u}+\partial_\mu F_{
u\lambda}+\partial_
u F_{\lambda\mu}\) contains pairs of second derivatives with opposite signs. Each pair cancels because partial derivatives commute. This is the covariant form of \(
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0\) and \(
abla	imes\mathbf E+\partial\mathbf B/\partial t=0\).} \optional_details{Splitting the covariant equations into the usual Maxwell equations}{The index \(
u=0\) part of \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0j^
u\) gives Gauss's law. The spatial choices \(
u=i\) give the Ampere-Maxwell law. The cyclic identity gives the two homogeneous equations: no magnetic monopoles and Faraday's law. The compact tensor equations are therefore the four familiar Maxwell equations written without choosing a special frame.}

title: Explanation
body: Maxwell's equations are not just four formulas to memorize; they are the local rules governing the electromagnetic field. They connect sources to fields and also allow fields to propagate as waves. In covariant notation, much of the structure becomes shorter: sources enter through the four-current, and the antisymmetric field tensor carries the electric and magnetic components together. If the sources vanish in a region, the equations still have nontrivial wave solutions. That is how light appears as a self-propagating electromagnetic disturbance rather than as a separate kind of object.

title: Definition
body: The Lorenz gauge is the covariant gauge condition \[ \partial_\mu A^\mu=0 \] imposed on the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential}. It selects a convenient representative from a gauge-equivalent family of potentials without changing the physical \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}.

title: Derivation
body:
Because of \cref{Gauge invariance}{sr.gauge_invariance}, potentials related by \(A_\muightarrow A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda\) describe the same field tensor. The \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential} therefore contains redundant descriptive freedom. The Lorenz gauge fixes part of that freedom by imposing the Lorentz-covariant scalar condition \[ \partial_\mu A^\mu=0. \] With this condition, the potential form of \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations} simplifies to a wave equation with source, schematically \(\Box A^\mu=\mu_0 j^\mu\) in SI conventions. \optional_details{Applying the Lorenz gauge to Maxwell's equations}{In terms of the potential, the sourced Maxwell equation contains terms of the form \(\Box A^
u-\partial^
u(\partial_\mu A^\mu)=\mu_0j^
u\), up to sign conventions. The Lorenz gauge sets \(\partial_\mu A^\mu=0\), so the second term disappears. What remains is a wave equation for each component of the potential: schematically \(\Box A^
u=\mu_0j^
u\).} \optional_details{Lorenz gauge versus Lorentz invariance}{The Lorenz gauge is named after Ludvig Lorenz, not Hendrik Lorentz. The condition is nevertheless Lorentz-covariant because \(\partial_\mu A^\mu\) is a scalar contraction. If it is zero in one inertial frame, it is zero in every Lorentz-related inertial frame.}

title: Explanation
body: The Lorenz gauge is a choice that makes the potential description cleaner without changing the physical field. Gauge conditions can feel suspicious at first: are we changing the physics? No. We are choosing one representative from many equivalent potentials, much like choosing convenient coordinates. The Lorenz gauge condition \(\partial_\mu A^\mu=0\) is especially useful because it respects Lorentz covariance and turns Maxwell's equations for the potential into a wave-equation form. Remember the spelling: Lorenz gauge, not Lorentz transformation.

title: Definition
body: Gauge invariance is the freedom to change the electromagnetic potential by \[ A_\mu\rightarrow A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda \] without changing the physical electromagnetic field. The \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} remains invariant under this transformation.

title: Derivation
body:
The invariance follows from the construction of the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}. Under \(A_\muightarrow A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda\), \[ F_{\mu
u}ightarrow \partial_\mu(A_
u+\partial_
u\Lambda)-\partial_
u(A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda). \] The added terms cancel because partial derivatives commute: \[ \partial_\mu\partial_
u\Lambda-\partial_
u\partial_\mu\Lambda=0. \] Therefore \(F_{\mu
u}\), and hence the physical \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}, is unchanged. \optional_details{Expanding the gauge transformation term by term}{After the transformation \(A_\mu	o A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda\), the new field tensor is \(F'_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u+\partial_\mu\partial_
u\Lambda-\partial_
u A_\mu-\partial_
u\partial_\mu\Lambda\). Grouping the original terms gives \(F_{\mu
u}\), and the remaining two second-derivative terms cancel. Therefore \(F'_{\mu
u}=F_{\mu
u}\).} \optional_details{Why commuting partial derivatives makes the cancellation work}{For a sufficiently smooth scalar function \(\Lambda\), the order of partial differentiation does not matter: \(\partial_\mu\partial_
u\Lambda=\partial_
u\partial_\mu\Lambda\). The gauge-added part of \(F_{\mu
u}\) is the difference between these two equal quantities. That is why a pure gradient in the potential has no electromagnetic field tensor.}

title: Explanation
body: Gauge invariance says the potential has redundancy: different \(A_\mu\) fields can produce the same \(F_{\mu\nu}\). This can be hard to accept because we are used to different mathematical descriptions meaning different physical situations. Here the field tensor is the observable electromagnetic object, and the potential has extra descriptive freedom. An analogy is choosing coordinates on a map: changing coordinates changes the labels, not the terrain. Gauge invariance is deeper than that analogy, but it helps with the first conceptual step: not every change in the potential is a physical change.

title: Definition
body: The four-current \(j^\mu\) combines charge density and current density into one relativistic \cref{Four-vectors}{sr.four_vectors}: \[ j^\mu=(c\rho,\mathbf j). \] It is the source appearing in covariant \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations}.

title: Derivation
body:
The four-current is built by packaging local charge density and ordinary current density into a four-vector. Since charge density is the time component of charge flow and \(\mathbf j\) is the spatial flux of charge, the covariant object is \[ j^\mu=(cho,j_x,j_y,j_z). \] Its transformation law is the \cref{Four-vectors}{sr.four_vectors} transformation law. Local conservation is expressed by its four-divergence, \(\partial_\mu j^\mu=0\), developed in \cref{Charge conservation}{sr.charge_conservation}. \optional_details{From continuity equation to \(\partial_\mu j^\mu=0\)}{The ordinary continuity equation is \(\partialho/\partial t+
abla\cdot\mathbf j=0\). With \(j^\mu=(cho,\mathbf j)\) and \(\partial_\mu=(\partial/(c\partial t),
abla)\), the four-divergence is \(\partial_\mu j^\mu=(1/c)\partial(cho)/\partial t+
abla\cdot\mathbf j\). This is exactly the ordinary continuity equation.} \optional_details{Why \(cho\) is the time component}{The spatial current \(\mathbf j\) has units of charge per area per time. Multiplying charge density \(ho\) by \(c\) gives the same dimensions, because \(cho\) is charge per volume times distance per time. It also makes \(j^\mu\) transform as a four-vector when charge flow is viewed from different inertial frames.}

title: Explanation
body: The four-current packages charge density and current density into one relativistic source object. Charge density alone is not enough because different observers disagree about densities and currents when charges are moving. What one observer calls mostly charge density, another may partly describe as current. The four-current keeps the bookkeeping together, just as four-momentum keeps energy and momentum together. In a wire, the lab frame and a frame moving with charges can assign different \(\rho\) and \(\mathbf j\), but they are related as components of \(j^\mu\).

title: Definition
body: Minimal coupling is the standard prescription for introducing electromagnetic interaction into a charged particle's dynamics by replacing ordinary momentum structure with the gauge-covariant combination involving the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential}, commonly \(p_\mu-eA_\mu\).

title: Derivation
body: The prescription is guided by \cref{Gauge invariance}{sr.gauge_invariance} and the existence of the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential}. For a charged particle, one adds the simplest local interaction term between the particle worldline and the potential, proportional to \[ e A_\mu dx^\mu. \] Equivalently, in momentum language the free momentum is replaced by the gauge-covariant combination \[ p_\mu\rightarrow p_\mu-eA_\mu. \] Varying the minimally coupled action gives the \cref{Lorentz force law}{sr.lorentz_force_law}. \optional_details{Why \(eA_\mu dx^\mu\) is a scalar interaction}{The displacement \(dx^\mu\) is a four-vector and \(A_\mu\) is a covector. Contracting them gives \(A_\mu dx^\mu\), a Lorentz scalar. Multiplying by the charge \(e\) gives an interaction term that all inertial observers agree how to include in the action.} \optional_details{From worldline coupling to \(p_\mu-eA_\mu\)}{In Hamiltonian or wave-mechanical language, the interaction with the potential is captured by replacing the free canonical momentum with a gauge-covariant combination. The subtraction \(p_\mu-eA_\mu\) is arranged so that a gauge change in \(A_\mu\) can be compensated by the corresponding phase or canonical transformation. This keeps observable quantities gauge-invariant.}

title: Explanation
body: Minimal coupling is the economical way to make a charged particle interact with electromagnetism. Instead of inventing a separate force rule first, we insert the vector potential into the particle's action or momentum structure. The phrase 'minimal' means no unnecessary extra terms: use the simplest local, gauge-compatible coupling. This also explains why canonical momentum and mechanical momentum can differ. In the nonrelativistic limit, the Lagrangian picks up terms involving \(\phi\) and \(\mathbf A\), and varying it gives the Lorentz force.

title: Definition
body: The Lorentz force law is the relativistic equation of motion for a charged particle in an electromagnetic field. In covariant form it relates the rate of change of \cref{Momentum four-vector}{sr.momentum_four_vector} to the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} and the particle's \cref{Velocity four-vector}{sr.velocity_four_vector}.

title: Derivation
Explanation
body: The Lorentz force law is the bridge from field to particle motion. In three-vector form it says electric fields push charges along the field and magnetic fields deflect moving charges sideways. In covariant form the same statement becomes one compact equation involving \(F^\mu{}_{\nu}\), four-velocity, and four-momentum. The compact notation is not just elegance; it shows that electric and magnetic forces are components of one relativistic interaction. A charge at rest in an electric field and a moving charge curving in a magnetic field are two familiar faces of the same law.

title: Definition
body: Charge conservation is the local statement that electric charge cannot appear or disappear. In relativistic notation it is written as the continuity equation for the \cref{Four-current}{sr.four_current}: \[ \partial_\mu j^\mu=0. \]

title: Derivation
body:
Charge conservation follows from the sourced \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations}. Taking the divergence of \[ \partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0 j^
u \] gives \[ \partial_
u\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0\partial_
u j^
u. \] The left-hand side vanishes because \(F^{\mu
u}\) is antisymmetric while the double derivative is symmetric in \(\mu\) and \(
u\). Therefore \[ \partial_\mu j^\mu=0. \] This is the covariant continuity equation for the \cref{Four-current}{sr.four_current}. \optional_details{Why symmetric derivatives contracted with an antisymmetric tensor vanish}{The double derivative \(\partial_
u\partial_\mu\) is symmetric in the two indices because partial derivatives commute. The field tensor \(F^{\mu
u}\) is antisymmetric, so swapping \(\mu\) and \(
u\) changes the sign of \(F\) but not of the derivative operator. A quantity equal to its own negative must be zero, so \(\partial_
u\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=0\).} \optional_details{Relating \(\partial_\mu j^\mu=0\) to charge conservation}{Expanding the four-divergence gives \(\partialho/\partial t+
abla\cdot\mathbf j=0\). This says that charge density in a small volume can decrease only if current flows out through the boundary, and can increase only if current flows in. Integrating over a volume gives the usual statement that total charge changes by the negative of the outward current flux.}

title: Explanation
body: Charge conservation is local bookkeeping. It does not merely say the total charge of the universe stays fixed; it says charge cannot disappear from a small box unless current flows through the boundary. The continuity equation expresses that point-by-point accounting. In Maxwell theory it also follows from the antisymmetry of the field tensor, so it is built into the consistency of the equations. If charge density in a small region decreases, the equation demands an outward current. The charge went somewhere; it did not vanish at an event.

title: Definition
body: The electromagnetic energy density is the energy per unit volume carried by the \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}. In SI units it is \[ u=\frac12\left(\epsilon_0 E^2+\frac{1}{\mu_0}B^2\right), \] where \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) are the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} and \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field}.

title: Derivation
body: The energy density is obtained as the time-time component of the electromagnetic \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor}. In a chosen inertial frame, decomposing the field tensor into the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} and \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field} gives \[ T^{00}=u=\frac12\left(\epsilon_0 E^2+\frac{1}{\mu_0}B^2\right). \] Thus the energy stored locally in the field is built from the squared electric and magnetic field strengths. \optional_details{Computing \(T^{00}\)}{The \(00\) component is selected because it represents energy density in the chosen inertial frame. Substitute the electric and magnetic pieces of \(F_{\mu\nu}\) into the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor and keep \(\mu=\nu=0\). Cross terms cancel by antisymmetry, leaving the sum of squared field strengths with the SI factors \(\epsilon_0\) and \(1/\mu_0\).} \optional_details{Why the energy density is quadratic in field strengths}{A field and its negative should store the same amount of energy, so the energy density cannot be linear in \(\mathbf E\) or \(\mathbf B\). The leading local scalar-like quantities are \(E^2\) and \(B^2\). This matches the work required to build up fields gradually from zero, where doubling the field strength quadruples the stored energy.}

title: Explanation
body: Electromagnetic fields store energy locally. That is a major conceptual step if you first met fields only as devices for exerting forces on charges. The energy is not just in the particles; it can be in the field between them and can move through space. The formula \(u=\tfrac12(\epsilon_0E^2+B^2/\mu_0)\) says stronger fields carry more energy density. In a plane wave, the electric and magnetic contributions are equal, so the field energy is shared between the two components. This energy density is one component of the larger energy-momentum tensor.

title: Definition
body: The Poynting vector \(\mathbf S\) describes electromagnetic energy flux: the rate at which field energy flows through unit area. In SI units, \[ \mathbf S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B. \] It is closely related to the momentum density of the electromagnetic field.

title: Derivation
body: The Poynting vector is obtained from the mixed time-space components of the electromagnetic \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor}. When those components are decomposed into the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} and \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field}, the energy-flow result from \cref{Field energy}{sr.electromagnetic_field} gives \[ \mathbf S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B. \] The corresponding field momentum density is \[ \mathbf g=\frac{\mathbf S}{c^2}. \] \optional_details{From \(T^{0i}\) to \(\mathbf S\)}{The components with one time index and one space index describe the flow of energy or the density of momentum, depending on index placement and convention. For the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor, evaluating these mixed components in terms of \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) gives a vector proportional to \(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\). In SI units the energy flux is \(\mathbf S=(1/\mu_0)\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\).} \optional_details{Why field momentum density is \(\mathbf S/c^2\)}{Energy flux has units of energy per area per time. Momentum density has units of momentum per volume, and for radiation energy and momentum are related by \(E=pc\). The covariant stress-energy tensor packages these quantities consistently, leading in SI units to \(\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2\).}

title: Explanation
body: The Poynting vector tells you where electromagnetic energy is going. Energy density says how much field energy is stored in a region; \(\mathbf S\) says how that energy flows through space. The cross product \(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\) is a direction cue as well as a formula: in a plane wave with \(\mathbf E\) along \(y\) and \(\mathbf B\) along \(z\), \(\mathbf S\) points along the direction of propagation. Relativity ties this energy flux to momentum density, so field energy flow also means field momentum.

title: Definition
body: The electromagnetic stress-energy tensor is the electromagnetic-field instance of the general \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor}. It combines electromagnetic energy density, momentum density, energy flux, and stresses into one Lorentz-covariant tensor.

title: Derivation
body:
For the electromagnetic field, the stress-energy tensor is constructed algebraically from the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} and the \cref{Metric tensor}{sr.metric_tensor}. With the \(+---\) convention and suppressing unit-dependent constants, a common form is \[ T^{\mu
u}=-F^{\mu\lambda}F^
u{}_{\lambda}+ rac14\eta^{\mu
u}F^{\alpha eta}F_{\alpha eta}. \] This is the electromagnetic specialization of the general \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor}. \optional_details{Why the tensor is quadratic in \(F_{\mu
u}\)}{Field energy should not change sign when the electromagnetic field is reversed, so it must be even in the fields. The simplest Lorentz-covariant expressions are quadratic contractions of \(F_{\mu
u}\). The stress-energy tensor uses these quadratic combinations while keeping two free indices so it can describe energy density, momentum density, and stress.} \optional_details{Recovering energy density from \(T^{00}\)}{To find the energy density measured in a chosen inertial frame, set \(\mu=
u=0\) in the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor. The time-space components of \(F\) contribute terms involving \(E^2\), while the spatial components contribute terms involving \(B^2\). With SI constants restored, the result is \(T^{00}= rac12(\epsilon_0E^2+B^2/\mu_0)\).}

title: Explanation
body: The stress-energy tensor may sound abstract, but it is a complete local accounting sheet for electromagnetic energy and momentum. The time-time part is energy density, the mixed parts describe energy flux and momentum density, and the spatial parts describe stresses: momentum flowing across surfaces. Radiation pressure is a concrete example. Light hitting a surface carries momentum, so it can push. Different observers split the tensor into density, flux, and stress differently, but they are decomposing the same covariant object.

title: Definition
body: The energy-momentum tensor \(T^{\mu\nu}\) is a rank-two tensor that describes the density and flow of energy and momentum through spacetime. Its conservation equation, \[ \partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0, \] expresses local conservation of energy and momentum for an isolated system.

title: Derivation
body:
The energy-momentum tensor is derived from spacetime translation symmetry using \cref{Noether's theorem}{sr.noether_theorem}. If the action is unchanged under constant shifts \[ x^\mu ightarrow x^\mu+\epsilon^\mu, \] then there is a conserved current for each spacetime direction. These four conserved currents are assembled into \(T^{\mu
u}\), with the conservation law \[ \partial_\mu T^{\mu
u}=0. \] For fields described by a Lagrangian density \(\mathcal L(\phi_a,\partial_\mu\phi_a)\), the canonical form is \[ T^\mu{}_{
u}= rac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}\partial_
u\phi_a-\delta^\mu{}_{
u}\mathcal L. \] This form may be improved or symmetrized when needed, especially for gauge fields. For electromagnetism, the physically useful symmetric tensor is constructed from the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}. With the \(+---\) metric convention and suppressing unit-dependent constants, \[ T^{\mu
u}=-F^{\mu\lambda}F^
u{}_{\lambda}+ rac14 \eta^{\mu
u}F^{\alpha eta}F_{\alpha eta}. \] This tensor packages electromagnetic energy density, momentum density, and stresses into one Lorentz-covariant object. \optional_details{From translations to four conserved currents}{A spacetime translation has four independent parameters: one for time and three for space. Noether's theorem gives one conserved current for each parameter. Placing those four currents side by side gives the two-index object \(T^{\mu
u}\), where one index labels the current direction and the other labels which component of energy-momentum is being transported.} \optional_details{Deriving the canonical tensor}{Under a small translation, the field changes by \(\delta\phi_a=-\epsilon^
u\partial_
u\phi_a\). Substituting this transformation into Noether's theorem gives a current proportional to \((\partial\mathcal L/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a))\partial_
u\phi_a\) plus a term from translating the volume element. The result is \(T^\mu{}_{
u}=(\partial\mathcal L/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a))\partial_
u\phi_a-\delta^\mu{}_{
u}\mathcal L\).} \optional_details{Why stress-energy can be symmetrized}{The canonical tensor is not always symmetric and may not be the most useful tensor for gauge fields. One can often add an improvement term whose divergence is identically zero, so the conserved total energy and momentum do not change. The improved tensor can be made symmetric and gauge-invariant, which is why electromagnetism is usually described with the symmetric tensor built from \(F_{\mu
u}\).}

title: Explanation
body: The energy-momentum tensor generalizes the idea of energy and momentum conservation to fields and continuous systems. A field can have energy spread through space, momentum flowing from one region to another, and stresses across surfaces. All of that local bookkeeping is held in \(T^{\mu\nu}\). The conservation equation \(\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\) says energy-momentum is not disappearing at a point; it is balanced by flow. For electromagnetism, \(T^{00}\) gives field energy density, while other components encode Poynting flux, momentum density, and pressure-like stresses.

title: Definition
body: Electromagnetic waves are propagating source-free disturbances of the \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}. In a chosen frame they appear as coupled oscillations of the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} and \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field}, travelling at speed \(c\) in vacuum.

title: Derivation
body:
Electromagnetic waves follow from source-free \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations}. In a region where the \cref{Four-current}{sr.four_current} vanishes, Maxwell's equations imply a \cref{Wave equation}{sr.wave_equation} for the field or for the potential in a suitable gauge: \[ \Box A^\mu=0. \] Plane-wave solutions have electric and magnetic components transverse to the propagation direction, and the speed of propagation is fixed by the invariant light speed \(c\). \optional_details{Deriving the source-free wave equation}{In a region with no charge or current, \(j^\mu=0\). Maxwell's equations then reduce, in Lorenz gauge, to \(\Box A^\mu=0\). Equivalently, taking curls and time derivatives of the usual three-vector Maxwell equations gives \((1/c^2)\partial^2\mathbf E/\partial t^2-
abla^2\mathbf E=0\) and the same equation for \(\mathbf B\).} \optional_details{Why electromagnetic waves are transverse}{For a plane wave moving in direction \(\mathbf k\), the source-free equations include \(
abla\cdot\mathbf E=0\) and \(
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0\). Substituting a plane wave turns these into \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf E=0\) and \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf B=0\). Thus both fields are perpendicular to the propagation direction.}

title: Explanation
body: An electromagnetic wave is a self-sustaining disturbance of one electromagnetic field, not two independent waves called electric and magnetic. Maxwell's equations link the changing electric and magnetic components so the disturbance propagates at \(c\) in vacuum. In a plane wave, \(\mathbf E\), \(\mathbf B\), and the direction of travel are mutually perpendicular, and the Poynting vector points along the propagation direction. The wave carries energy and momentum, which is why light can heat a surface or exert radiation pressure.

title: Definition
body: The relativistic wave equation is a field equation involving the d'Alembertian operator \[ \Box=\partial_\mu\partial^\mu=\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2. \] For electromagnetism, it describes propagating solutions of the vector potential or fields.

title: Derivation
body:
The electromagnetic wave equation is obtained from \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations}. Writing the field in terms of the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential} and imposing the \cref{Lorenz gauge}{sr.lorenz_gauge}, \(\partial_\mu A^\mu=0\), the sourced equation becomes schematically \[ \Box A^\mu=\mu_0 j^\mu. \] The operator \(\Box\) is formed using the \cref{Metric tensor}{sr.metric_tensor}. In source-free regions where the \cref{Four-current}{sr.four_current} vanishes, this reduces to \[ \Box A^\mu=0, \] whose solutions describe \cref{Electromagnetic waves}{sr.electromagnetic_waves}. \optional_details{Applying Lorenz gauge to the potential equation}{Starting from \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0j^
u\) and writing \(F^{\mu
u}=\partial^\mu A^
u-\partial^
u A^\mu\), we get \(\partial_\mu\partial^\mu A^
u-\partial^
u(\partial_\mu A^\mu)=\mu_0j^
u\). The first term is \(\Box A^
u\). In Lorenz gauge the second term is zero, so the equation becomes \(\Box A^
u=\mu_0j^
u\), up to sign convention.} \optional_details{Plane-wave solutions of \(\Box A^\mu=0\)}{Try a solution \(A^\mu=\epsilon^\mu e^{i(k\cdot x)}\). Applying \(\Box\) brings down a factor proportional to \(-k_\mu k^\mu\). The wave equation therefore requires \(k_\mu k^\mu=0\), meaning the wave four-vector is null. This corresponds to propagation at speed \(c\).}

title: Explanation
body: The wave equation is the mathematical pattern for finite-speed propagation. With the \(+---\) metric, the d'Alembertian has one time part and three spatial parts: \(\Box=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\nabla^2\). That sign structure is what makes light-cone propagation appear. In electromagnetism, choosing the Lorenz gauge turns the potential equations into a clean wave equation. In a source-free region, plane waves satisfy \(\omega=ck\), which is the compact statement that the disturbance moves at speed \(c\).

title: Definition
body: Radiation reaction is the back-reaction force on an accelerating charged particle caused by the energy and momentum it radiates away as electromagnetic waves.

title: Derivation
body: An accelerating charge emits \cref{Electromagnetic waves}{sr.electromagnetic_waves}. Those waves carry energy and momentum, described locally by the \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor}. Conservation of total energy and momentum then requires the charged particle's motion to be modified: the particle loses energy-momentum to the field it radiates. Radiation reaction is the correction to the motion beyond the applied \cref{Lorentz force law}{sr.lorentz_force_law}. \optional_details{Energy-momentum balance for an accelerating charge}{An accelerating charge creates fields that propagate away as radiation. Those fields carry energy and momentum, measured by the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor. If total energy-momentum is conserved, the particle cannot keep the same motion it would have had under only an external Lorentz force; some energy-momentum has left with the radiation.} \optional_details{Why the Lorentz force is not the whole story}{The Lorentz force describes how external electromagnetic fields push a charge. But the charge also creates its own field, and when it accelerates that self-field contains outgoing radiation. Radiation reaction is the correction that accounts for the back-effect of the charge's own radiated field on its motion.}

title: Explanation
body: Radiation reaction is difficult because the charge is affected by the field it creates. The ordinary Lorentz force describes how an external field acts on a charge. But an accelerating charge emits electromagnetic waves, and those waves carry energy and momentum away. Conservation then says the particle's motion must reflect that loss. A driven electron, for example, radiates while it oscillates, so some work done on it leaves as radiation rather than remaining as particle energy. The details are subtle because self-interaction can lead to unphysical runaway or pre-accelerating solutions if handled carelessly.

title: Definition
body: Lorentz invariance is the statement that the laws of physics have the same form in all inertial frames related by \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations}. Equivalently, physical equations should be expressible using Lorentz-covariant objects and invariant contractions.

title: Derivation
body: Lorentz invariance is the modern mathematical expression of the \cref{Principle of relativity}{sr.principle_of_relativity} in Minkowski spacetime. The relevant transformations are the \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations}, defined by preserving the \cref{Metric tensor}{sr.metric_tensor}: \[ \Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta. \] Objects such as \cref{Four-vectors}{sr.four_vectors}, the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}, and the \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor} transform in ways that preserve tensor equations between inertial frames. \optional_details{How \(\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta\) preserves scalar products}{For two four-vectors \(A\) and \(B\), the scalar product is \(A^T\eta B\). After a Lorentz transformation it becomes \((\Lambda A)^T\eta(\Lambda B)=A^T\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda B\). Using \(\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta\), this reduces back to \(A^T\eta B\). Thus scalar products and tensor equations built from them keep their invariant content.} \optional_details{What it means for an equation to be Lorentz-covariant}{An equation is Lorentz-covariant if both sides transform in the same way under Lorentz transformations. For example, if both sides are four-vectors, then changing frames multiplies both sides by the same \(\Lambda^\mu{}_{\nu}\). Therefore an equation true in one inertial frame remains true in every inertial frame, even though the component values may change.}

title: Explanation
body: Lorentz invariance is the demand that the form of physical law does not depend on which inertial observer writes it down. This does not mean every observer measures the same components. They usually do not. It means the equations relate objects that transform consistently, so all observers describe the same physics. Tensor notation is helpful because it makes this structure visible: if both sides of an equation are tensors of the same type, covariance is built in. For example, \(p_\mu p^\mu=m^2c^2\) is invariant, while Maxwell's equations in tensor form are covariant.

title: Definition
body: Gauge fixing is the choice of one representative potential from a family of gauge-equivalent potentials. It removes redundant descriptive freedom associated with \cref{Gauge invariance}{sr.gauge_invariance} without changing the physical electromagnetic field.

title: Derivation
body: Gauge fixing is possible because \cref{Gauge invariance}{sr.gauge_invariance} says that many potentials describe the same physical field. The \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential} may be changed while leaving the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} and hence the \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field} unchanged. A gauge condition adds an extra equation selecting a convenient representative. The \cref{Lorenz gauge}{sr.lorenz_gauge}, \(\partial_\mu A^\mu=0\), is one such choice and is useful because it respects \cref{Lorentz invariance}{sr.lorentz_invariance}. \optional_details{Gauge fixing as choosing a representative}{Gauge-related potentials describe the same physical field tensor, so they are like many different descriptions of one electromagnetic situation. A gauge condition adds an extra rule that selects one convenient representative from that family. The choice can simplify calculations without changing \(F_{\mu\nu}\) or any gauge-invariant observable.} \optional_details{Residual gauge freedom after imposing Lorenz gauge}{A gauge transformation changes \(\partial_\mu A^\mu\) by \(\Box\Lambda\). If the Lorenz gauge already holds, it will still hold after the transformation provided \(\Box\Lambda=0\). Therefore Lorenz gauge does not remove all gauge freedom; it leaves residual transformations whose gauge function satisfies the homogeneous wave equation.}

title: Explanation
body: Gauge fixing is choosing a convenient representative from many physically equivalent potentials. The danger is to think the gauge choice is an extra physical assumption. It is not; it is a way to remove redundant description. The field tensor remains the same. This is similar in spirit to choosing coordinates, though gauge symmetry has its own physics. The Lorenz gauge is a useful example because it preserves Lorentz covariance and simplifies Maxwell's equations for the potential to a wave-equation form, \(\Box A^\mu=\mu_0j^\mu\).
